answer:
HYPOTHESIS (associational, data-grounded): Among black NLSY79 respondents, incarceration between 1985 and 1994 is associated with substantially worse wealth outcomes at every baseline-wealth tier, and the damage differs by tier. In absolute dollars the associated shortfall is largest for respondents who started with higher positive wealth (jailed men in the top positive tier show a median 1985→1996 change of about −$7,000 to −$8,000 vs about +$12,500 for non-jailed peers, a jail gap of roughly −$15,000), but in proportional terms the harshest outcome is concentrated at the bottom: jailed respondents who began with low positive wealth (≤ $5,300, the median positive 1985 wealth) typically lost all of it by 1996 (median relative change −100%, ending at median $0), while comparable non-jailed respondents grew their wealth roughly five-fold (median relative change +525%). In the zero-wealth tier, jailed respondents show no median wealth accumulation by 1996 and materially lower mean accumulation than non-jailed peers (e.g., jailed black men ~$7,900 vs ~$18,500), and sex-adjusted regressions find a significant negative jailed coefficient in every tier (p ≤ 0.02). A formal cross-tier interaction test (penalty larger at lower baseline wealth) is not statistically significant in absolute-dollar terms (interaction p = 0.07–0.17), so the tier gradient is descriptive rather than statistically confirmed in levels — but the relative (proportional) collapse at the bottom tiers is unambiguous in the medians. All statements are associations, not causal effects.

KEY RESULTS (n = 3,013 black respondents; 159 jailed, 5.3%; male jailed rate 9.8% vs female 1.0%)

Tier sizes (baseline 1985 wealth): negative n=183, zero n=1,133, positive-low n=847 (0 < w < $5,300), positive-high n=850. Terciles/quartiles were degenerate because the 25th–33rd percentiles of 1985 wealth are $0; the four-tier scheme was used as primary and quartiles as sensitivity.

Jailed vs not-jailed counts per tier × sex (cell-size instability is visible, especially for women): negative — 0/117 women, 7/66 men; zero — 13/618 women, 56/515 men; pos-low — 2/437 women, 42/410 men; pos-high — 1/376 women, 38/474 women... (exact table in script output: pos-high women 1 jailed of 376, men 38 of 474). Female jailed cells are 0–13 observations; female results are reported but flagged as unreliable.

Change 1985→1996, medians (winsorized means in parentheses):
- negative tier: not-jailed +$5,648 (+$43,399 men) vs jailed +$3,700 (+$10,847 men); MWU p = 0.57 (n_jailed=7).
- zero tier: both medians $0; means differ (jailed men +$7,856 vs not-jailed +$18,543); MWU p < 0.001; sex-adjusted OLS jailed coef −$11,700 (p = 0.018).
- pos-low tier: not-jailed +$6,770 (+$32,775 men) vs jailed −$1,000 (+$9,827 men); MWU p = 0.003; OLS jailed coef −$24,287 (p < 0.001); jailed median relative change −100% vs +382% (men) / +525% (pooled) for non-jailed.
- pos-high tier: not-jailed +$12,535 (+$51,608 men) vs jailed −$7,038 (−$6,135 men); MWU p < 0.001; OLS jailed coef −$56,236 (p < 0.001); jailed median relative change −84% vs +54%.

DiD-style jail gap in median change 1985→1996: negative −$1,948; zero $0 (medians uninformative in the zero tier); pos-low −$7,770; pos-high −$14,775 — the absolute gap grows with baseline wealth, while the relative gap is catastrophic only at the bottom.

Interaction (OLS, sex-adjusted, change 1985→1996): jailed main effect −$39,067 (p < 0.001, pos-high reference); jail×zero +$11,730 (p = 0.17); jail×pos-low +$14,257 (p = 0.072). Not significant: no statistically confirmed evidence that the absolute dollar penalty is larger at lower baseline wealth; if anything the point estimates suggest the absolute penalty grows with baseline wealth while proportional loss is worst at the bottom.

Sensitivity (1985-wealth quartiles, ties at 0 collapsed): jailed respondents in the two upper quartiles show median changes of −$1,400 and −$8,000 vs +$9,300 and +$7,052 for non-jailed — same direction as the primary scheme.

Robustness: winsorization at the 1st/99th percentile of the black sample affected 62 of 3,013 rows per wave (~2%). Extreme negatives were flagged, not dropped: 31 rows per wave fall below the 1st percentile; raw minima are −$45,922 (1985), −$91,647 (1990 winsorized base) and −$949,81... (the full-sample raw minimum was −$866,400 in 1990; within the black sample the minima above). These extreme debts are kept in raw statistics and flagged as possible coding artifacts or genuine debt.

CAUSAL CAVEATS (verbatim, as approved): (1) ever_jailed is a coarse 1985–1994 proxy — no timing, duration, repeat, or severity; (2) selection is severe: incarceration is not random and correlates with pre-existing disadvantage partly visible in baseline wealth (jailed blacks already show lower 1985 median: 320 vs 764), so estimates are associations, not causal effects; (3) composite wealth construction (which five variables, negative-value handling, top-coding) is unknown; (4) no income variable — baseline wealth proxies income; (5) attrition/survey nonresponse unmeasurable here; (6) tiny jailed cell sizes in some tiers (especially black women) → unstable estimates; (7) possible wealth outliers/extreme debts dominate means.

WORKFLOW (executed): loaded CSV (12,013 rows, no missing values, no ID column, wide format); restricted to race == "black" (n = 3,013); winsorized each wealth wave at the black-sample 1st/99th percentiles (62 rows/wave affected) and flagged 31 extreme-negative rows per wave; constructed primary baseline tiers negative/zero/positive-low/positive-high using the median of positive 1985 wealth ($5,300) with 1985-wealth quartiles as a sensitivity check; computed absolute changes 1985→1990 and 1985→1996, relative changes for positive baselines, and 1996 levels; compared jailed vs not-jailed within every tier × sex cell (medians, winsorized means, Mann–Whitney U when both cells ≥ 5); pooled within-tier sex-adjusted OLS (HC3) of change 1985→1996 on jailed + male; computed DiD-style jail gaps in change by tier and a cross-tier jail×tier interaction; reported jailed/non-jailed counts per tier × sex.

LIMITATIONS: no respondent ID (1,899 exact-duplicate rows assumed to be distinct respondents); female jailed cells too small for inference (0–13 cases); zero-tier medians are uninformative (all $0) so mean-based and regression evidence carries that tier; the cross-tier interaction in absolute dollars is not statistically significant; "hipanic" spelling in the race column suggests upstream data-processing quirks; zero wealth may conflate true zeros with coded missingness.

In absolute dollars the shortfall grows with baseline wealth (DiD-style gaps: -1,948 / 0 / -7,770 / -14,775 across tiers), but the cross-tier interaction is not statistically significant (p = 0.07-0.17), so the tier gradient in levels is descriptive. payload.workflow: 1) Inspected data (12,013 rows x 6 cols, no missing values, no ID; wide format; wealth can be negative). 2) Restricted to black respondents (n=3,013; 159 jailed, 5.3%; male 9.8% vs female 1.0%). 3) Winsorized wealth levels at black-sample 1st/99th percentiles per wave (62 rows/wave affected; 31 extreme-negative rows per wave flagged, not dropped). 4) Built primary baseline (1985) tiers negative/zero/positive-low/positive-high using the median of positive 1985 wealth ($5,300) because terciles/quartiles degenerate at 0; quartile variant run as sensitivity. 5) Computed absolute changes 1985->1990 and 1985->1996, relative changes for positive baselines, and 1996 levels. 6) Compared jailed vs not-jailed within every tier x sex cell via medians, winsorized means, and Mann-Whitney U tests (both cells >= 5); reported jailed/non-jailed counts per tier x sex. 7) Pooled within-tier sex-adjusted OLS (HC3) of change 1985->1996 on jailed + male. 8) DiD-style jail gaps in change by tier and cross-tier jail x tier interaction OLS. 9) Stated associational caveats: coarse 1985-1994 ever_jailed proxy with unmeasured timing/severity; non-random selection into incarceration; unknown composite-wealth construction; no income variable so baseline wealth proxies income; tiny female jailed cells; unmeasurable attrition; possible extreme-debt coding artifacts.
